title: From fasting to building
hook: many hammer the first nail of the sukkah as Yom Kippur ends

segments.voice: Yesterday, Neilah, the closing gate. Your line was one long blast. Did your day end with a long breath and a hope? Today, what happens right after that blast. Day six hundred fifty-eight.

Yom Kippur is over. Stars are out. People pour out of the synagogue, dizzy with hunger, heading for bagels and orange juice. And in some backyards, before anyone has even sat down to eat, there's a strange sound. Tap, tap, tap. Someone is out in the dark with a hammer and a flashlight, banging in a single nail, or setting up one pole. Then they go inside and eat. They've started building a hut.
screen: `STARS OUT, FAST OVER.` → `TAP, TAP, TAP.` → `ONE NAIL, THEN DINNER.`

segments.voice: The hut is a sukkah, the temporary booth for the festival of Sukkot. Leviticus sets Yom Kippur on the tenth of the month and Sukkot on the fifteenth: five days apart. The Torah says: "Ye shall dwell in booths seven days." Rabbi Moshe Isserles, the great Ashkenazi authority, records the custom: right after Yom Kippur, begin building the sukkah, so as to go from one mitzvah to the next. Some just hammer one nail that night, a token. Others put up the whole frame. The idea behind it is old. A psalm says of the faithful: "They go from strength to strength." Later teachers read it as a rule of life. Don't leave a gap after something holy. When you finish one good thing, start the next while the energy is still warm. And look at the contrast. For ten days the focus was inward: judgment, books, confession, a day without food. Now the very next act is outward and physical: wood, nails, branches, a roof you can see the stars through. The year doesn't stay in the synagogue. The calendar itself moves the mood from awe to joy, from fasting to building. Some readers add a gentle reason. Just after Yom Kippur, a person is as clean as they'll ever be, and the first thing they do is start a home. Not a palace. A hut with branches for a roof, begun with one nail, in the dark.
screen: `DWELL IN BOOTHS SEVEN DAYS.` · `FROM ONE MITZVAH TO THE NEXT.` · `FROM STRENGTH TO STRENGTH.` · `FROM INWARD TO OUTWARD.` · then, large: `FROM FASTING TO BUILDING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: start something right after finishing. Think of something you've just completed, or will finish today: a task, a meal, a piece of work, even this lesson. Before the glow fades, decide the very first step of the next good thing. Make it tiny: one nail. Then, if you can, do that tiny step right after this sit, before you check anything else. If you pray, you can ask for strength to go from strength to strength. The bell holds the time.
From fasting to building. The custom of starting the sukkah as soon as Yom Kippur ends, going straight from one mitzvah to the next.

Your line: from fasting to building. A week of ask before the day, release the vows, dressed in white, once a year, even Nineveh, one long blast. Today, when you finish one thing, hammer the first nail of the next. Day six hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Many Jews begin building their sukkah on the night Yom Kippur ends, even if only by hammering one nail or setting up one pole, then finish it in the days before Sukkot.
